author: Anonymous (traditionally attributed to Clement of Rome)
addressee: A Christian congregation, addressed as 'brothers' and 'brothers and sisters'
occasion: A preacher exhorts a congregation to repentance, pure living, and endurance in view of coming judgment, presenting his own written appeal for them to heed.
argument: The homily calls believers to think of Christ as God and judge of the living and the dead, and to repay his saving mercy with confession enacted in deeds, not just words. It urges them to abandon the world, keep the flesh pure as God's temple, and repent while there is still time. The preacher warns that the present age and the coming age are enemies, and that only those who do God's will will receive the promised kingdom. He encourages endurance amid present suffering by pointing to the future reward and the certainty of judgment.

outline.move: Exhorts believers to think of Christ as God and judge, and recalls the mercy by which he saved them from idolatry and death.
Interprets Isaiah's barren woman as the church, once desolate but now fruitful, and explains Christ's call of sinners.
Defines confessing Christ as obeying his commands and honoring him with heart and deeds, not lips alone.
Calls believers to leave the world, fear God rather than persecutors, and serve God rather than mammon.
Uses the athletic contest and the potter's clay to urge repentance while there is still opportunity.
Argues that the flesh will be judged and raised, so it must be kept pure as God's temple.
Warns against those who prefer present pleasure to future promise and mislead others, and against double-mindedness, urging patient hope in God's promises.
Explains the Lord's saying about the two becoming one as truthfulness, inner purity, and freedom from lust.
Warns that the name of God is blasphemed among the nations when believers fail to love even their enemies.
Presents the church as the spiritual body of Christ, pre-existing creation and manifested in the flesh.
Commends self-control and faithfulness, and ranks almsgiving above fasting and prayer as means of repentance before the coming day of judgment.
Urges mutual correction and perseverance, and describes the fate of the wicked and the reward of the righteous at Christ's appearing.
The preacher humbly includes himself among sinners still striving for righteousness.
Concludes with a plea to heed the written appeal, endure present trials, and trust God's delayed reward, ending in doxology.

key_terms.sense: The human flesh or body, which must be kept pure and will be raised
The Holy Spirit, or the spiritual reality prefigured by the flesh
The church, understood as the spiritual body of Christ, pre-existing creation
Repentance, turning from sin with the whole heart
The seal, likely baptism, which must be kept unspotted
The kingdom of God, the coming reign to be awaited and entered
Recompense or return given to God or received from him
Double-mindedness, wavering between faith and doubt
Mammon, wealth or worldly gain opposed to God
The appearing of God or Christ at the day of judgment
Incorruption, the immortal life promised to the faithful
The earthly copy or type that points to a heavenly original
Sojourning, the temporary stay of believers in this world

scripture: The author quotes the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) and cites prophets by name (Isaiah, Ezekiel). Psalm numbering follows the Septuagint where applicable. Modern citations should use standard English Bible names and numbering, noting Septuagint usage where it differs.
uncertain: The exact date of composition; mid-2nd century is a scholarly estimate.
The identity of the author; the attribution to Clement is traditional and not from the text itself.
The precise location of the congregation addressed.
Whether the work was originally delivered orally as a homily or composed as a written exhortation.
The exact meaning of the saying about the two becoming one in section 12.
Whether 'the seal' refers specifically to baptism or more broadly to Christian identity.

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: section 9: καὶ γὰρ εἶπεν ὁ κύριος: Ἀδελφοί μου οὗτοί εἰσιν οἱ ποιοῦντες τὸ θέλημα τοῦ πατρός μου.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The Lord (Jesus) also speaks in section 9, which is missing from the list. The sections should be ["3", "4", "5", "6", "8", "9", "12", "13", "17"].

_unresolved_facts.claim: The double-minded, how_marked: Quoted as those who say 'These things we heard long ago...', sections: ["11"]
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: section 11: οἱ λέγοντες: Ταῦτα πάλαι ἠκούσαμεν καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν πατέρων ἡμῶν, ἡμεῖς δὲ ἡμέραν ἐξ ἡμέρας προσδεχόμενοι οὐδὲν τούτων ἑωράκαμεν.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The double-minded are not introduced with a direct 'they say' formula but are described as part of a prophetic quotation: "Ταλαίπωροί εἰσιν οἱ δίψυχοι... οἱ λέγοντες" (section 11). The how_marked should indicate this is embedded within a prophetic quotation, not a direct quotation of the double-minded themselves.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The nations, how_marked: Described as saying it is a myth and a delusion, in indirect discourse, sections: ["13"]
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: section 13: ἔνθεν εἰς βλασφημίαν τρέπονται, λέγοντες εἶναι μῦθόν τινα καὶ πλάνην.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The nations are introduced with a participial construction "λέγοντες" (saying), which is more direct than pure indirect discourse. The how_marked should indicate participial/direct quotation construction.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The faithless at judgment, how_marked: Quoted as saying 'Woe to us, because you were...', sections: ["17"]
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: section 17: Οὐαὶ ἡμῖν, ὅτι σὺ ἦς, καὶ οὐκ ᾔδειμεν καὶ οὐκ ἐπιστεύομεν καὶ οὐκ ἐπειθόμεθα τοῖς πρεσβυτέροις τοῖς ἀναγγέλλουσιν ἡμῖν περὶ τῆς σωτηρίας ἡμῶν.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The quotation is incomplete. The full quotation continues: "καὶ οὐκ ἐπειθόμεθα τοῖς πρεσβυτέροις τοῖς ἀναγγέλλουσιν ἡμῖν περὶ τῆς σωτηρίας ἡμῶν." The claim truncates the quotation and omits the reference to the elders.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The righteous at judgment, how_marked: Quoted as saying 'There will be hope for the one who has served God...', sections: ["17"]
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: section 17: ὅτι ἔσται ἐλπὶς τῷ δεδουλευκότι θεῷ ἐξ ὅλης καρδίας.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The brief's rendering "There will be hope for the one who has served God" is inaccurate. The Greek says "ἔσται ἐλπὶς τῷ δεδουλευκότι θεῷ ἐξ ὅλης καρδίας" — "there will be hope for the one who has served God with his whole heart." The brief omits "with his whole heart" (ἐξ ὅλης καρδίας), which is significant given the homily's emphasis on whole-hearted service.
